report.tagline: A London-based payments company that processes online card and wallet payments for large global businesses like Uber, eBay and Spotify.
report.simpleSummary: When you pay for an Uber ride or a Spotify subscription, a company in the background has to take your card details, check with your bank, and move the money to the business. Checkout.com does that job for big online companies. It focuses on large merchants that sell in many countries and care about every small improvement in how many payments go through. It does not sell to shoppers directly; shoppers never see it.

overview.whatItDoes: Checkout.com lets businesses accept card payments, digital wallets like Apple Pay and local payment methods online, all through one connection. It also handles payouts, fraud checks and identity checks. It is built for large merchants that want high success rates and detailed data.
howItWorks: A business connects its website or app to Checkout.com through an API.
When a shopper pays, Checkout.com sends the request to the card network (Visa, Mastercard) and the shopper's bank to approve it.
It runs fraud checks with its own tools in milliseconds.
As an 'acquirer' in many countries, it holds licences to settle money directly to the merchant, which removes middlemen.
Merchants see detailed data on why payments fail and tools to raise approval rates.
It is adding support for payments made by AI shopping agents, such as Google's Universal Commerce Protocol.
overview.valueProposition: More payments approved, at lower cost, with one global platform and deep data, for businesses where a 1% gain in approval is worth millions.

businessModel.summary: Checkout.com charges merchants a small fee on each payment, on top of the card network and bank fees it passes through. It earns more from extras like fraud tools, payouts and identity checks.

revenueStreams.detail: A markup on each payment, usually a small percentage or fixed fee above interchange and scheme fees.
Fraud detection, identity checks and data tools.
Fees for sending money and converting currency.

businessModel.pricing: Custom pricing for each merchant, usually interchange++ (the card network and bank costs plus a Checkout.com fee). Not public.
costDrivers: Card network and bank fees (passed through to merchants)
Technology and infrastructure for very high uptime
Licences and compliance in many countries
businessModel.unitEconomics: Take a $100 online payment. The merchant might pay about $1.50 in total. Most of that, about $1.20 to $1.35, goes to the shopper's bank and the card network. Checkout.com keeps maybe 15 to 30 cents. With $300 billion in volume, a keep rate of about 0.3% to 0.4% would mean net revenue of roughly $1 billion or more. Big merchants push this markup down, so Checkout.com relies on high volume and selling extras.

howTheyGetUsers: Winning share of volume from merchants who use several providers
Reputation for approval rates and data
New hubs in the US and Brazil
whatBringsUsersBack: Payments run continuously; merchants stay if performance is good
New features like payouts and identity checks
growth.moat: Its own acquiring licences, a high-performance platform, and deep relationships with big merchants. Rivals like Stripe and Adyen have similar strengths, so the moat is performance and price rather than a lock-in.

competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Checkout.com focuses on large enterprises and custom pricing; Stripe is broader.

competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Adyen is larger and stronger in-store; Checkout.com focuses on online.

northStar.metric: Value of successful payments processed for merchants
northStar.why: Merchants care about getting paid. Successful payment value captures both volume and approval quality. That is what makes it a good north star metric: it moves only when customers get real value.

pmLessons: In B2B infrastructure, small improvements in a core metric like approval rate are worth millions to customers.
Valuation is not success. Checkout.com's value fell but the business kept growing and became profitable.
Focusing on a segment (large global merchants) makes product choices clearer.
New channels like AI agents create openings for infrastructure players.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you raise the approval rate for a merchant?
interviewQuestions.hint: Break down declines by cause: fraud, issuer, technical. Ideas: network tokens, retries, data sharing. Guardrail: fraud.

interviewQuestions.question: Checkout.com vs Stripe: how would you position Checkout.com?
interviewQuestions.hint: Segment: enterprise vs everyone. Strengths: performance, pricing, licences. Weaknesses: breadth.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you prepare for agentic commerce?
interviewQuestions.hint: Define agent payments. Issues: identity, consent, fraud. Product: tokens, limits, logs. Metric: agent volume.

interviewQuestions.question: What metrics would you put on the merchant dashboard?
interviewQuestions.hint: Approval rate, fraud rate, cost per payment, speed. Prioritise what merchants act on.

interviewQuestions.question: Should Checkout.com serve small businesses?
interviewQuestions.hint: Weigh the cost to serve, competition, brand focus and revenue.
